Advanced biofuels include heating oil, jet fuel, naphtha, renewable gasoline, renewable natural gas (RNG), and renewable propane (detailed fuel volume data are available in Appendix A). This figure only includes the volume and electricity produced, not the associated coproducts. Figure ES-2 shows the development of the biofuels industry from 2015 through 2024. Renewable diesel, a drop-in fuel, experienced tremendous growth in capacity and consumption in recent years due to the conversion of existing refineries. Biodiesel’s contribution has largely remained at a similar level, with a slight decrease in recent years that is likely a result of the growing renewable diesel market. Ethanol remains the top contributor to the bioeconomy. Data for advanced biofuels were obtained from the EPA’s public Renewable Fuel Standard data and were based on volume. Other advanced biofuels include biogas, butanol cellulosic diesel, cellulosic gasoline, cellulosic heating oil, naphtha, renewable heating oil, RNG, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF; also referred to as synthetic aviation fuel). This dataset includes small volumes of imported advanced biofuels. Economic and job impacts from the bioeconomy are considerable. Industry organizations that fund studies use economic input-output models to estimate economic and job impacts. The Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) funds an annual study of ethanol’s impact on the economy. The study found the 2024 impacts to gross domestic product, household income, and taxes were $53 billion, $28 billion, and $10 billion, respectively (RFA 2025c). Ethanol’s direct and induced jobs were more than 56,000 and 258,000, respectively. A study based on 2024 biodiesel, renewable diesel, and SAF markets found an economic impact of $42 billion and support of 107,400 jobs and $5.8 billion in wages paid (GlobalData 2025). RNG’s contribution included an estimated 55,000 jobs and $7 billion to gross domestic product. The average wage was $66,890, and 75% of jobs did not require a college degree (Guidehouse 2024). SAF, made from non-petroleum feedstocks, is a drop-in fuel that reduces emissions from air transportation. SAF can be blended at different levels with limits of 10% to 50%, depending on the feedstock and how the fuel is produced.. At the time this report was prepared, there were five commercial domestic producers and one international producer supplying the U.S. market. 2024 consumption was 112 million gallons, a substantial increase from 1.8 million gallons in 2018 (EPA 2025d).
